A small fact makes a difference.
Our class is making a blog about school memories. Ruby thinks her grandfather has a good story to share, so she invited him to talk to us. He tells us that his old classroom had wooden desks and a very large map. He also says that pupils wrote everything in notebooks because there were no tablets. We asked questions and took short notes. Later, our group typed a document about his first school trip. Sam wrote that the trip happened in 1960, but Ruby was not sure about the year. We did not want to guess. Our teacher asked her grandfather to check it. He said the trip was in 1961. We corrected the file before adding it to the blog. Jo says that the new story is clear, but she thinks two words may be difficult for younger readers. We added a small vocabulary list with simple meanings. Then Sam read the story aloud while we followed the text. Reading it helped us notice one sentence that was too long. We divided it into two shorter sentences. I hope the class will enjoy our blog. I have learned that telling a story means choosing useful details as well as remembering events. Checking one small fact can make the whole story better.
